topic.title: The Pipeline Wall: Is Midstream Natural Gas Capacity -- Not Turbines or the Grid -- AI Data Centers' Next Power Bottleneck?
topic.trigger: Williams Companies, Kinder Morgan and Energy Transfer's Q2 2026 earnings (late July-early August 2026) each disclosed record or near-record gas-infrastructure project backlogs explicitly tied to AI data-center and power-generation demand -- Williams closing a $5.5B Haynesville-to-Gulf-Coast acquisition (Momentum Midstream) and raising its long-term EBITDA growth target to 11%+ CAGR through 2030, Kinder Morgan reporting 60%+ of its $9.6B backlog tied to power/LDC demand, and Energy Transfer disclosing 6+ Bcf/d of contracted data-center/power-plant pipeline capacity -- while FERC's unanimous May 21, 2026 rulemaking to overhaul its natural gas blanket-certificate program (the first such overhaul in 20 years) is a direct regulatory response to a pre-existing multi-year interstate-pipeline permitting backlog. This is a midstream gas-transport layer distinct from the gas-turbine manufacturing bottleneck (examined 2026-09-16) and the electric-grid interconnection bottlenecks (PJM BYONC, 2026-08-28; ghost-demand queue freezes, 2026-09-06) this pipeline has previously examined.

questions.primary: Is long-haul interstate natural gas pipeline transport capacity -- distinct from gas-turbine manufacturing and electric-grid interconnection, both already examined by this pipeline -- now an independent, binding constraint on how fast new gas-fired power can reach AI data centers, or is midstream capacity being added fast enough (aided by capital-light laterals and FERC's 2026 permitting reform) to keep this from becoming a durable structural bottleneck?
sub: How much of Williams', Kinder Morgan's and Energy Transfer's record 2026 project backlogs and raised guidance is directly tied to data-center and power-generation gas demand, and on what timeline does that capacity actually come online?

Does the multi-year interstate-pipeline certification and construction timeline (a pre-reform ~465-day FERC certificate backlog and a July 2030 target in-service date for Williams' 950 MMcf/d Transco Power Express expansion) constitute a binding constraint distinct from the gas-turbine bottleneck this pipeline has already documented?

How much faster can capital-light laterals and behind-the-meter gas-supply projects (e.g., Energy Transfer's Abilene lateral, Williams' Atlas and Socrates projects) come online relative to long-haul interstate pipeline expansions, and does that materially blunt the bottleneck?
Does FERC's May 2026 blanket-certificate rulemaking meaningfully shorten the permitting timeline for new interstate gas capacity, or is relief still years away?

How wide is the gap between headline data-center gas-demand forecasts (a 3-20 Bcf/d-by-2030 analyst range) and what midstream companies and analysts such as East Daley say is realistically achievable given pipeline-capacity and turbine/tie-in constraints?

thesis: Record 2026 project backlogs and raised guidance at Williams Companies, Kinder Morgan and Energy Transfer -- the three largest US midstream gas-pipeline operators -- driven explicitly by AI data-center and associated power-generation demand, combined with a pre-existing FERC interstate-pipeline certificate backlog (~465 days average pre-reform) and multi-year in-service timelines for major expansions (Williams' 950 MMcf/d Transco Power Express not targeted online until July 2030), indicate that long-haul, FERC-certificated interstate natural gas pipeline transport capacity has become a distinct, low-elasticity, hard-to-substitute structural bottleneck on how fast new gas-fired power can reach AI data centers -- one layer removed from the gas-turbine manufacturing bottleneck and the electric-grid interconnection bottlenecks this pipeline has already examined. Unlike interstate mainline expansions, capital-light laterals and behind-the-meter gas-supply projects that bypass FERC's certificate process (Williams' Atlas, targeted in service by end-2026; Energy Transfer's Abilene lateral, completed within a single quarter) show markedly higher supply elasticity, and FERC's unanimous May 2026 blanket-certificate rulemaking directly targets the binding permitting constraint -- leaving the bottleneck's durability genuinely contested, especially given a wide (3-20 Bcf/d by 2030) analyst range on how much real incremental gas demand data centers will ultimately create.

facts.statement: Williams Companies reported Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA of $1.921 billion (+6% YoY) and year-to-date adjusted EBITDA of $4.175 billion (+10%), raised full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance by $200 million to $8.3-8.5 billion, and raised its long-term EBITDA growth target to 11%+ CAGR through 2030 (from 10%+), citing data-center and power demand.

Williams closed a strategic acquisition of Momentum Midstream for up to $5.5 billion (including approximately $2 billion in Williams common stock), adding roughly 6 Bcf/d of gas-gathering capacity and 4 Bcf/d of pipeline capacity in the Haynesville Shale and connecting it to Gulf Coast LNG and power demand.

Williams' FERC-approved Transco Power Express expansion project will add 950 MMcf/d of firm transportation capacity from Alabama/Georgia into Virginia to serve data-center and power-generation demand, with a target in-service date of July 1, 2030 -- more than three and a half years from this report's publication.

Williams' Atlas project will provide up to 164 MMcf/d of pipeline capacity for a large Northeast data-center customer and is targeted for service by the end of 2026, while its $1.6 billion Will-Power 'Socrates' behind-the-meter power-and-pipeline project in Ohio (backed by a 10-year power purchase agreement) is targeted for completion in the second half of 2026 -- both far faster than the multi-year Power Express interstate mainline expansion.

Incoming Williams CEO Chad Zamarin, who succeeded Alan Armstrong on July 1, 2026, said that 'there is certainly going to be some tempering of pace based on the supply chain' regarding the buildout of data-center-driven gas and power projects.

Kinder Morgan's project backlog stood at $9.6 billion at the end of Q2 2026 (down $500 million from Q1 2026 as roughly $660 million of projects, including the Tennessee Gas Pipeline Cumberland Project and a Gulf Coast Express expansion, were placed into service); natural gas projects made up approximately 92% of the backlog, and more than 60% of the backlog is tied to power-generation and local-distribution-company demand. Q2 2026 adjusted EBITDA was $2.199 billion (+12% YoY) and adjusted EPS was $0.37 (+32% YoY).

Kinder Morgan's Natural Gas Pipeline Company of America (NGPL) is preparing to file a FERC application for the approximately $200 million Amarillo Expansion, which would add up to 550,000 Dth/d (about 0.55 Bcf/d) of firm transportation capacity for Texas Panhandle data-center development; the project is fully subscribed under long-term contracts but is not targeted for service until Q3 2028 -- roughly two years from filing.

Energy Transfer raised full-year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to $18.8-19.1 billion and disclosed multiple long-term agreements with Oracle to supply approximately 900,000 Mcf/d (about 0.9 Bcf/d) of natural gas to three US data centers, two of them in Texas, plus two additional customers adding a combined 100 MMcf/d to existing contracts for power-plant/data-center sites in Texas during Q2 2026.

Energy Transfer's Hugh Brinson Pipeline entered commercial service ahead of schedule and was expected to reach full Phase 1 capacity by September 1, 2026; the company also completed an additional 14-mile lateral off that pipeline in Abilene, Texas within the same quarter, and said most of its data-center-linked projects are tied to behind-the-meter power plants specifically to reduce exposure to electric-grid interconnection delays.

As of its June 2026 investor presentation, Energy Transfer had contracted more than 6 Bcf/d of pipeline capacity serving data centers and the power plants behind them, with an 18-year weighted-average contract life and more than $25 billion of expected firm-transportation revenue.

On May 21, 2026, FERC voted 5-0 to propose the most consequential overhaul of its natural gas pipeline blanket-certificate program in roughly 20 years (Docket RM25-12-001), which would roughly double the cost thresholds allowing pipeline companies to build or modify infrastructure without case-by-case FERC approval, expand the categories of projects eligible for streamlined authorization, and for the first time extend the blanket-certificate framework to LNG facilities; FERC separately extended a temporary cost-limit waiver for pipeline projects to May 31, 2028 pending the final rule.

As of a mid-2025 industry analysis of FERC's own public project data, 15 natural gas pipeline projects had completed environmental review but remained in a certificate-decision backlog averaging 465 days -- well over a year -- a pre-existing permitting delay that predates and helps motivate FERC's 2026 blanket-certificate rulemaking.

East Daley Analytics forecasts 4.2-6.1 Bcf/d of incremental data-center natural gas demand by 2030 across roughly 290 projects totaling about 81 GW, with data centers representing an estimated 2.5 Bcf/d of demand by the end of 2026, up from about 0.8 Bcf/d a year earlier; the firm says it has 'consistently limited' its own demand estimate (to about 4.8 Bcf/d by 2030) specifically because of pipeline-capacity constraints and long queues for gas turbines and transmission interconnection tie-ins, calling that figure 'far short of' a roughly 15 Bcf/d unconstrained potential.

Credible forecasters disagree sharply on the scale of AI-driven natural gas demand: S&P Global's base case is +3 Bcf/d with an upside near 6 Bcf/d by 2030 depending on how fast supporting infrastructure is built, other analysts cite a 3-20 Bcf/d range by 2030, and Wood Mackenzie projects power-sector gas demand rising 17 Bcf/d by the mid-2030s with data centers accounting for roughly two-thirds of that power-sector growth through 2035.

The US Energy Information Administration's September 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook projects natural gas power-sector consumption will reach a record 46.1 Bcf/d in summer 2027, driven by data-center and industrial demand growth concentrated in Texas and Virginia, about 4% above the 2021-2025 five-year summer average.

inferences.statement: Because Williams, Kinder Morgan and Energy Transfer are all simultaneously raising backlogs, guidance and long-term growth targets on the same data-center-driven gas demand while their flagship long-haul interstate expansions (Transco Power Express, NGPL's Amarillo Expansion) still take until 2028-2030 to enter service, near-term supply of certificated interstate pipeline capacity is running behind disclosed demand specifically at that layer, even as the companies' overall project backlogs grow.

FERC's unanimous, first-in-20-years overhaul of the blanket-certificate program is itself evidence that federal regulators view permitting delay -- not physical construction capability -- as a principal binding constraint on the gas infrastructure needed for the AI/data-center buildout.

The markedly faster in-service timelines for behind-the-meter and lateral projects (Williams' Atlas by end-2026 and Socrates in H2 2026; Energy Transfer's Abilene lateral completed within a single quarter and its Hugh Brinson Pipeline ahead of schedule) versus multi-year interstate mainline expansions indicate supply elasticity is bifurcated by project type within the same midstream industry -- a pattern consistent with the bottleneck/Growth-Area splits this pipeline has documented in other AI-infrastructure supply chains.

The wide dispersion in analyst estimates of data-center gas demand (a 3-20 Bcf/d range by 2030) combined with East Daley's explicit self-discounting of its own forecast because of pipeline, turbine and interconnection-tie-in constraints suggests the true magnitude of realized (as opposed to announced or contracted) demand cannot yet be measured with confidence, echoing the 'ghost demand' overstatement pattern this pipeline documented in electric-grid interconnection queues.

unknowns: No hyperscaler or AI data-center operator has yet publicly and specifically attributed a project delay to interstate gas-pipeline transport capacity, as distinct from turbines, transformers, or electric-grid interconnection.

The precise share of midstream companies' disclosed 'data-center' gas demand that represents genuinely new incremental burn, versus re-contracted or re-routed existing supply, is not fully disclosed by any of the three companies examined.
Whether FERC's May 2026 blanket-certificate rulemaking will be finalized substantially as proposed, or narrowed after the public comment period, is not yet known.

Whether the pre-reform ~465-day FERC certificate backlog figure (based on mid-2025 data) has materially changed by September 2026 is not independently confirmed by any more recent tracking found in this research.

bottlenecks.node: Long-haul interstate natural gas pipeline transport capacity (FERC-certificated)
bottlenecks.rationale: Demand is Extreme: all three major midstream operators are raising backlogs and guidance on explicit data-center/power demand, and EIA projects record gas-power consumption. Supply elasticity is Low: FERC's pre-reform certificate backlog averaged 465 days, and flagship interstate expansions (Transco Power Express, NGPL's Amarillo Expansion) take until 2028-2030 to enter service even when fully subscribed. Substitutability is Hard because firm, dispatchable interstate gas transport to large new gas-fired power plants has no readily available near-term alternative at hyperscale (electric-grid interconnection and battery/nuclear alternatives face their own multi-year bottlenecks already documented by this pipeline). All three strict conditions are met.

Demand is equally extreme, but projects that bypass FERC's certificate process by using existing rights-of-way or serving a single behind-the-meter customer (Williams' Atlas and Socrates, Energy Transfer's Abilene lateral) have shipped in a single quarter to under two years -- materially higher elasticity than mainline expansions. Fails the Low-elasticity leg of the strict test.

bottlenecks.node: Gas gathering and basin-level processing capacity
bottlenecks.rationale: Gathering and processing capacity is scaling via M&A (Williams' $5.5B Momentum Midstream deal added 6 Bcf/d of Haynesville gathering) faster than certificated long-haul transport, and multiple competing basins and operators provide more substitutability. Fails the Low-elasticity and Hard-substitutability legs.

bear_case.argument: All three major midstream operators are simultaneously expanding via M&A, new mainline projects and fast-moving laterals, and FERC's unanimous reform push shows regulators actively working to remove the permitting constraint -- this could resolve into a temporary multi-year lag rather than a durable ceiling.

Analyst estimates of data-center gas demand span a wide 3-20 Bcf/d range by 2030, and East Daley explicitly discounts its own forecast below headline potential -- echoing the 'ghost demand' overstatement pattern this pipeline documented in electric-interconnection queues, meaning the true gap may be narrower than backlog growth suggests.

Incremental pipeline expansion capex is comparatively modest per unit of capacity (Kinder Morgan's NGPL Amarillo Expansion costs about $200 million for roughly 0.55 Bcf/d) versus fab-level or turbine-level capital intensity, and laterals/behind-the-meter projects have shipped in as little as one quarter.

FERC's 5-0 vote to overhaul the blanket-certificate program for the first time in 20 years directly targets the identified permitting bottleneck, and a temporary cost-limit waiver already extends relief to pipeline projects through May 2028.

Growing hyperscaler use of behind-the-meter generation, on-site solar/storage and (per this pipeline's prior HALEU and lithium-battery reports) nuclear and battery alternatives could reduce reliance on long-haul interstate gas transport specifically, even though those alternatives carry their own documented multi-year constraints.

kill_conditions.condition: FERC's interstate pipeline certificate backlog/average approval time shortens materially following the 2026 blanket-certificate reform
kill_conditions.metric: FERC-tracked pipeline certificate backlog and average decision time
kill_conditions.threshold: Average certificate backlog falls below roughly 180 days for two consecutive quarters

kill_conditions.condition: Verified/contracted data-center gas demand growth stalls well below the 3-6 Bcf/d base-case range
kill_conditions.metric: Aggregate disclosed contracted Bcf/d tied to data centers across Williams, Kinder Morgan and Energy Transfer
kill_conditions.threshold: Aggregate disclosed contracted growth flattens or declines for two consecutive quarters

kill_conditions.condition: Major interstate mainline expansions begin entering service on or ahead of schedule across multiple companies
kill_conditions.metric: Reported in-service dates versus original targets for Transco Power Express, NGPL Amarillo Expansion and comparable projects
kill_conditions.threshold: Two or more major expansions confirmed on schedule or ahead of schedule

kill_conditions.condition: AI hyperscaler capital-expenditure guidance decelerates materially
kill_conditions.metric: Aggregate hyperscaler capital-expenditure growth guidance (Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle)
kill_conditions.threshold: Aggregate guided capex growth decelerates materially quarter over quarter

validation_events.weakens_if: Guidance growth decelerates or Power Express/Atlas timelines slip

Note: this domain was blocked by the research environment's egress proxy; content is drawn from convergent search-result snippets of the company's own recap and corroborating trade-press coverage (Natural Gas Intel).

sources.claim: A mid-2025 industry analysis of FERC's own public project data found 15 natural gas pipeline projects with completed environmental review still awaiting a certificate decision, averaging 465 days in backlog.
sources.source_title: Arbo: "Examining the FERC Backlog and Looming Large Diameter Projects"
sources.quote_or_extract: There are 15 backlogged pipelines, with the average backlog time at well over a year (465 days at the time of the article); a project is defined as backlogged if its environmental review has been completed but the Commission has not issued a certificate or a denial. Note: this analysis predates FERC's May 2026 blanket-certificate rulemaking and is used here only as pre-reform baseline context; more recent backlog tracking was not found in this research.

sources.claim: Law-firm analyses corroborate that FERC's May 21, 2026 NOPR (Docket RM25-12-001) proposes the most consequential overhaul of the blanket-certificate program since 2006, roughly doubling cost thresholds and expanding eligible project categories.
sources.source_title: White & Case LLP: "FERC proposes to expand blanket certificate authorizations for natural gas pipelines"
sources.quote_or_extract: FERC's May 21, 2026 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (Docket No. RM25-12-001) proposes the most consequential overhaul of its natural gas pipeline permitting regulations in roughly 20 years, roughly doubling cost thresholds allowing streamlined blanket-certificate authorization and expanding the scope of eligible projects, including extending the framework to LNG facilities for the first time.

sources.claim: The EIA's September 2026 Short-Term Energy Outlook projects record natural gas power-sector consumption of 46.1 Bcf/d in summer 2027, driven by data-center and industrial demand growth concentrated in Texas and Virginia.
sources.source_title: U.S. Energy Information Administration: Short-Term Energy Outlook, September 2026
sources.quote_or_extract: In summer 2027, natural gas power consumption is projected to reach 46.1 Bcf/d, a new record driven by data-center and industrial growth concentrated in Texas and Virginia; the current forecast sits about 4% above the 2021-2025 five-year summer average. Note: this domain was blocked by the research environment's egress proxy; the figure is drawn from a convergent search-result snippet summarizing the official EIA outlook.

sources.claim: S&P Global's base case is +3 Bcf/d of data-center gas demand with an upside near 6 Bcf/d by 2030; other analysts cite a 3-20 Bcf/d range; Wood Mackenzie projects power-sector gas demand rising 17 Bcf/d by the mid-2030s with data centers accounting for roughly two-thirds of that growth through 2035.
sources.source_title: Data Center Dynamics: "S&P: Data center growth to precipitate natural gas demand in US" (aggregating S&P Global and Wood Mackenzie estimates)
sources.quote_or_extract: S&P Global estimates a base-case addition of 3 Bcf/d of data-center-driven natural gas demand, with an upside scenario approaching 6 Bcf/d by 2030 depending on how quickly supporting infrastructure can be built; other analysts cite a broader 3-20 Bcf/d range by 2030. Wood Mackenzie separately projects power-sector gas demand rising 17 Bcf/d by the mid-2030s, with data centers accounting for roughly two-thirds of power-sector gas demand growth through 2035.
